slides.title: Negative Exponent Law
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the whole lesson in one question: a negative exponent asks for the RECIPROCAL of a power, and the misconception is that it asks for the opposite. A board that swaps the two answers is the board to watch today.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Each entry is the previous one divided by 2. After 2⁰ = 1 the next division gives ½, then ¼, then ⅛. Students fill the last three cells before the rule is stated. The question to ask: is 2⁻¹ negative? (No — dividing 1 by 2 gives a positive half.)
OFF: 'Negative exponent, positive value. The sign of the exponent tells you to divide; it says nothing about the sign of the answer.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
State the law both ways: a power with a negative exponent is 1 over the same power with a positive exponent, and a negative exponent in a denominator moves up. Then the contrast that the state guide asks for explicitly: −b and b⁻¹ are different numbers. Write 5⁻², −5², (−5)² and −25 on the board and ask which are equal.
OFF: 'Reciprocal, not opposite. 5⁻² is one twenty-fifth. It is a small positive number, not a negative one.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Two roads again: apply the negative exponent law first and multiply the reciprocal out, or apply the product law directly by adding a negative. Same 216. Then the quotient: 9⁻⁵ ÷ 9³ = 9⁻⁸ — subtracting past zero is fine, and the answer is written with a positive exponent at the end.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Two negative exponents, different bases — so no product or quotient law applies. Ask: what does each negative exponent tell you to do?

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: The 2⁻³ moves down and becomes 2³; the 9⁻² moves up and becomes 9². Then evaluate. A student who gets 8/81 moved nothing and just dropped the signs; one who gets −81/8 made the exponent's sign the answer's sign.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches the sign-dropper (9/5) and the sign-flipper (−5/9). 5/9 is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Same base, so the quotient law applies: 0 − (−4). Ask what 0 minus negative 4 is before anyone writes.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Road 1: subtract the exponents, 0 − (−4) = 4. Road 2: 7⁰ is 1, and 1 over 7⁻⁴ is 7⁴ by the law's second form. 2401 both ways. A board with 7⁻⁴ subtracted the wrong way; a board with 1/2401 read the law backwards.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches −4 − (−6) done as −10 (a board with 1/(−8)¹⁰) and a dropped sign on the base (a board with −64 — but (−8)² is 64). 64 is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: The law, plain. A board with −8³ or −512 made the exponent's sign the value's sign — the confusion the guide's first task targets (−b vs b⁻¹).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Ruling 22's board: the width is there to be read past. Nothing in the question needs it. −128 and −14 (2 · −7) are the two wrong boards to name; a board with 25 in it read the wrong number.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: The second form of the law. A board with 1/100 applied the law to a power that was already in the denominator — it moved nothing.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: The base keeps its sign; the exponent supplies the reciprocal. A board with 1/8 dropped the base's sign; a board with −8 or 8 ignored the reciprocal.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic — the one that matters most today. A board full of B means Notes II did not land; go back to the pattern table and divide 1 by 5 out loud, twice.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. The law is unchanged; the only new thing is adding a negative. B is the board that read 'negative exponent' as 'subtract'.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Exponents that sum to zero. The reciprocal route gives 1/81 · 81 = 1 too. A board with 0 read 3⁰ as 0 — the Lesson 3.02 misconception resurfacing.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Subtracting past zero: −5 − 3 = −8, then rewrite. A board with 9⁻² added; a board with 9⁻⁸ has the right power but not the positive form that was asked for.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written. The book's own cool-down item, kept. Full credit: the correct value and the sentence 'a negative exponent means the reciprocal of the power, not a negative number'. A student who writes 'she forgot the parentheses' is thinking of (−5)², a different expression.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
